title: Venus: The Hottest Planet
summary: Why Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest planet, and how its thick toxic clouds, backward spin, and runaway greenhouse effect make it so.
poll: Venus would be a good planet for humans to visit one day.

versions.title: The Hottest Planet
versions.text:
Look up at dusk. Do you see a bright dot? It may be Venus. It does not blink. It is a planet. It goes round the sun. So do we. It is the next one out from the sun.

Venus is near the size of Earth. Some folks call it Earth's twin. But it is not like Earth at all once you look close.

Thick air wraps it all. The air is a gas. Thick clouds wrap it too. The clouds are not soft like ours. They hold a harsh acid.

The air and clouds trap heat. The heat can not get out. This makes Venus the hottest planet of all. It is even hotter than Mercury. But Mercury sits near the sun.

It is so hot there it could melt some metal. No one could stand on it.

Venus spins the wrong way. Most planets do not. It also spins so slow. One spin takes longer than one whole trip round the sun!

versions.title: The Hottest Planet

Venus is nearly the same size as Earth. Some people call it Earth's twin. But Venus is not made like Earth at all. Thick air covers it. The air is a gas called carbon dioxide. It is not like the air on Earth.

Thick clouds also cover Venus. The clouds are made of a harsh acid. They are not like clouds on Earth. The air and clouds trap heat near the ground. The heat can not get back out.

This makes Venus the hottest planet of all. It is even hotter than Mercury. Mercury sits closer to the sun. But Venus still wins for heat.

Venus is hot enough to melt some metal. No person could stand on it.

Venus also spins the wrong way. Most planets spin one way. Venus spins the other way. It spins very slow too. One full spin takes longer than one whole year on Venus!

On a clear night, you may see a bright dot in the sky. It does not blink. It could be Venus. Venus is a planet. Like Earth, it goes around the sun. It is the second planet from the sun.

Venus is almost the same size as Earth. People call it Earth's twin. But Venus is not like Earth once you look close. Thick air covers all of it. The air is a gas called carbon dioxide, so it is not like the air we breathe. Thick clouds cover Venus too, and they never seem to break apart.

Venus is best known for its thick, heavy air. The clouds are made of a harsh acid, not water like clouds on Earth. The air and clouds trap heat near the ground, so the heat can not get back out into space.

This trapped heat makes Venus the hottest planet of all. It is even hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury sits much closer to the sun. Venus is hot enough to melt some metal, and no person could ever stand on it.

Venus also spins the wrong way. Most planets spin one way, but Venus spins the other way. It also spins very slow.

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might see a bright dot in the sky. It does not blink. It could be Venus. Venus is a planet, and like Earth, it travels around the sun. It is the second planet from the sun. It is much closer to the sun than Earth is.

Venus is almost exactly the same size as Earth. This is why some call it Earth's twin. But Venus is not made like Earth at all. Thick air covers the whole planet. This air is a gas called carbon dioxide. It presses down much harder than the air we breathe. Thick clouds also cover Venus completely. These clouds never seem to break apart or clear away.

Venus is best known for this thick, heavy blanket of air. The clouds are made of a harsh acid. They are not gentle water drops like the clouds here on Earth. The air and clouds trap heat close to the ground. That heat has almost nowhere to escape back into space.

This trapped heat makes Venus the hottest planet in our solar system. In fact, Venus is even hotter than Mercury. This is true even though Mercury sits much closer to the sun. Venus is hot enough to melt certain metals. No person could ever survive standing on its surface.

Venus also spins in the wrong direction. While most planets spin one way, Venus spins the opposite way. It spins extremely slowly too.

A day on Venus means one full spin. That spin actually takes longer than one whole trip around the sun!

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet in Our Solar System
versions.text:
Just after sunset, you might see an extremely bright point of light low in the sky. That bright light is often Venus. Venus is the second planet from the sun. Because its clouds reflect sunlight so well, many people say Venus is the brightest planet we can see from Earth.

Venus is almost the same size as Earth. This is why scientists call it Earth's twin. But once researchers studied Venus with spacecraft, they found something surprising. The two planets are nothing alike underneath their clouds.

A thick blanket of gas covers the whole planet. Scientists call this blanket of gas the atmosphere. This atmosphere is made mostly of carbon dioxide. It presses down far harder than the air that covers Earth. Dense clouds also cover Venus completely. These clouds are made of a harsh acid, not gentle water drops like clouds on Earth.

This thick atmosphere traps heat near the surface. That heat cannot escape back out into space. Scientists call this the greenhouse effect. On Venus, this effect works so well that Venus becomes the hottest planet in the whole solar system. Venus is even hotter than Mercury. This is true even though Mercury sits much closer to the sun.

Venus also rotates in an unusual, backward direction. Most planets do not turn this way. Its spin is also very slow. A single day on Venus, one full spin, lasts longer than one whole Venus year. A year is the time it takes to orbit the sun.

Surface conditions on Venus are so harsh that no spacecraft lasts long there. Every craft that has landed has survived for only a short time before the heat and pressure destroyed it.

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet in Our Solar System
versions.text:
Just after sunset or just before sunrise, an observer might notice a very bright point of light low in the sky. That bright light is often Venus, the second planet from the sun. Because its dense clouds reflect so much sunlight back toward us, Venus is actually the brightest planet in our night sky.

Venus is almost exactly the same size as Earth, which is why scientists sometimes call it Earth's twin. However, once researchers studied Venus closely using orbiting and landing spacecraft, they discovered something surprising. The two planets are fundamentally nothing alike beneath their swirling, unbroken clouds.

An unusually thick blanket of gas surrounds the entire planet, made up mostly of carbon dioxide along with traces of sulfuric acid droplets in its clouds. This atmosphere presses down on the surface with about ninety times more force than Earth's air does at sea level. Unlike the gentle water drops that form clouds on Earth, Venus's clouds are made of this harsh, corrosive acid.

This thick atmosphere traps heat near the surface, keeping it from ever radiating back out into space. Scientists call this process the greenhouse effect, and on Venus it works at a truly extreme level. As a direct consequence, Venus has become the hottest planet in our solar system, with surface temperatures above four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Remarkably, Venus stays even hotter than Mercury, despite the fact that Mercury orbits much closer to the sun.

Venus also rotates in an unusual, backward direction, a motion astronomers call retrograde rotation. Its rotation is also astonishingly slow: a single day on Venus, meaning one complete spin, actually lasts longer than one entire Venus year, the time it takes to orbit the sun.

Because surface conditions are so harsh, every spacecraft that has ever landed there has survived only a brief time, generally less than two hours, before the extreme heat and crushing pressure destroyed its delicate instruments, proof of just how inhospitable the Venusian surface truly is.

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet in Our Solar System
versions.text:
Just after sunset or just before sunrise, an observer might notice a very bright point of light low in the sky. That bright light is often Venus, the second planet from the sun, and Earth's closest planetary neighbor. Because its dense clouds reflect so much sunlight back toward us, Venus is actually the brightest planet in our night sky.

Venus is almost exactly the same size as Earth, which is why scientists sometimes call it Earth's twin. However, once researchers studied Venus closely using orbiting and landing spacecraft, they discovered something surprising. The two planets are fundamentally nothing alike beneath their swirling, unbroken clouds.

An unusually thick blanket of gas surrounds the entire planet, made up mostly of carbon dioxide along with traces of sulfuric acid droplets in its clouds. This atmosphere presses down on the surface with about ninety times more force than Earth's air does at sea level, a pressure comparable to that found nearly a kilometer beneath Earth's oceans. Unlike the gentle water drops that form clouds on Earth, Venus's clouds are made of this harsh, corrosive acid, capable of damaging many materials it touches.

This thick atmosphere traps heat near the surface, keeping it from ever radiating back out into space. Scientists call this process the greenhouse effect, and on Venus it works at a truly extreme level, unmatched anywhere else in the solar system. As a direct consequence, Venus has become the hottest planet in our solar system, with surface temperatures above four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Remarkably, Venus stays even hotter than Mercury, despite the fact that Mercury orbits much closer to the sun and receives more direct sunlight.

Venus also rotates in an unusual, backward direction, a motion astronomers formally call retrograde rotation. Its rotation is also astonishingly slow: a single day on Venus, meaning one complete spin, actually lasts longer than one entire Venus year, the time it takes the planet to orbit the sun.

Because surface conditions are so harsh, every spacecraft that has ever landed there has survived only a brief time, generally less than two hours, before the extreme heat and crushing pressure destroyed its delicate instruments, proof of just how inhospitable the Venusian surface truly is to any visitor.

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet in Our Solar System
versions.text:
Just after sunset or just before sunrise, an attentive observer might notice a very bright point of light low in the sky. That bright light is often Venus, the second planet from the sun, and Earth's closest planetary neighbor. Because its dense clouds reflect such an enormous proportion of sunlight back toward us, Venus is actually the brightest planet in our entire night sky.

Venus is almost exactly the same size as Earth, which is why scientists sometimes call it Earth's twin. However, once researchers began studying Venus closely using orbiting and landing spacecraft, they discovered something rather surprising. The two planets are fundamentally nothing alike beneath their swirling, perpetual, unbroken clouds.

An unusually thick blanket of gas surrounds the entire planet, composed mostly of carbon dioxide along with persistent traces of sulfuric acid droplets suspended in its clouds. This atmosphere presses down on the surface with roughly ninety times more force than Earth's air exerts at sea level, a pressure comparable to that experienced nearly a kilometer beneath Earth's oceans. Unlike the gentle water droplets that form clouds on Earth, Venus's clouds consist entirely of this harsh, corrosive acid, capable of damaging numerous materials upon contact.

This thick atmosphere traps solar heat near the surface, keeping it from ever effectively radiating back out into space. Scientists call this process the greenhouse effect, and on Venus it operates at a truly extreme, runaway level, unmatched anywhere else in the solar system. As a direct consequence, Venus has become the hottest planet in our solar system, with surface temperatures exceeding four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, more than hot enough to melt lead. Remarkably, Venus stays even hotter than Mercury, despite the undeniable fact that Mercury orbits considerably closer to the sun and receives substantially more direct sunlight.

Venus also rotates in an unusual, backward direction, a motion astronomers formally term retrograde rotation. Its rotation is also astonishingly slow: a single day on Venus, meaning the duration of one complete spin, actually lasts considerably longer than one entire Venus year, the time required for the planet to orbit the sun.

Because surface conditions there are so extraordinarily harsh, every spacecraft that has ever successfully landed on Venus has survived only a brief interval, generally less than two hours, before the extreme heat and crushing pressure destroyed its delicate instruments, clear proof of just how inhospitable the Venusian surface truly is to any visitor.

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet in Our Solar System
versions.text:
Just after sunset or just before sunrise, an attentive observer might notice a very bright point of light low in the sky. That bright light is often Venus, the second planet from the sun, and Earth's closest planetary neighbor. Because its dense clouds reflect such an enormous proportion of sunlight back toward us, Venus is actually the brightest planet in our entire night sky, outshining every star nearby.

Venus is almost exactly the same size as Earth, which is precisely why scientists sometimes call it Earth's twin. However, once researchers began investigating Venus closely using orbiting and landing spacecraft, they discovered something rather surprising. The two planets are fundamentally and profoundly nothing alike beneath their swirling, perpetual, unbroken clouds.

An unusually thick blanket of gas surrounds the entire planet, composed predominantly of carbon dioxide along with persistent traces of corrosive sulfuric acid droplets suspended throughout its clouds. This atmosphere presses down on the surface with roughly ninety times more pressure than Earth's atmosphere exerts at sea level, a magnitude comparable to that experienced nearly a kilometer beneath Earth's oceans. Unlike the gentle water droplets that form clouds on Earth, Venus's clouds consist entirely of this harsh, corrosive acid, capable of damaging numerous materials upon prolonged contact.

This extraordinarily thick atmosphere traps solar heat near the surface, preventing it from ever effectively radiating back out into the vacuum of space. Scientists refer to this process as the greenhouse effect, and on Venus it operates at a truly extreme, runaway level, unmatched anywhere else in the solar system. As a direct consequence, Venus has become the hottest planet in our solar system, with surface temperatures exceeding four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, more than sufficient to melt lead. Remarkably, Venus manages to stay even hotter than Mercury, despite the undeniable fact that Mercury orbits considerably closer to the sun and receives substantially more direct solar radiation per unit of surface area.

Venus also rotates in an unusual, backward direction relative to nearly every other planet, a motion astronomers formally designate as retrograde rotation. Its rotation is also astonishingly slow: a single day on Venus, meaning the duration of one complete axial spin, actually lasts considerably longer than one entire Venus year, the time required for the planet to complete an orbit of the sun.

Because surface conditions there are so extraordinarily harsh, every spacecraft that has ever successfully landed on Venus has survived only a brief interval, generally less than two hours, before the extreme heat and crushing atmospheric pressure destroyed its delicate instruments, clear proof of just how inhospitable the Venusian surface truly remains to any potential visitor.

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet in Our Solar System
versions.text:
Venus, the second planet from the sun and Earth's closest planetary neighbor, is often the extremely bright point of light visible low in the sky just after sunset or just before sunrise; because its dense clouds reflect so much sunlight back toward observers, Venus ranks as the brightest planet in our entire night sky, outshining every star nearby.

Almost exactly the same size as Earth, Venus is sometimes called Earth's twin by scientists, yet once researchers began investigating the planet closely using orbiting and landing spacecraft, they discovered that the two worlds are fundamentally nothing alike beneath Venus's swirling, perpetual, unbroken clouds.

An unusually thick atmosphere, composed predominantly of carbon dioxide with persistent traces of corrosive sulfuric acid suspended throughout its clouds, surrounds the entire planet; this atmosphere presses down on the surface with roughly ninety times more pressure than Earth's atmosphere exerts at sea level, comparable to the pressure experienced nearly a kilometer beneath Earth's oceans. Unlike the gentle water droplets forming clouds on Earth, Venus's clouds consist entirely of harsh, corrosive acid capable of damaging numerous materials upon prolonged contact.

This extraordinarily thick atmosphere traps solar heat near the surface, preventing it from radiating back out into the vacuum of space; scientists call this the greenhouse effect, and on Venus it operates at a truly extreme, runaway level unmatched anywhere else in the solar system. Consequently, Venus has become the hottest planet in the solar system, with surface temperatures exceeding four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, sufficient to melt lead; remarkably, Venus remains hotter than Mercury despite the fact that Mercury orbits considerably closer to the sun and receives substantially more direct solar radiation per unit of surface area.

Venus also rotates in an unusual, backward direction relative to nearly every other planet, a motion astronomers formally term retrograde rotation; its rotation is also astonishingly slow, since a single Venusian day, the duration of one complete axial spin, actually lasts considerably longer than one entire Venus year, the time required to complete a single orbit around the sun.

Given how extraordinarily harsh surface conditions are, every spacecraft that has successfully landed on Venus has survived only a brief interval, generally under two hours, before extreme heat and crushing atmospheric pressure destroyed its instruments, clear proof of just how inhospitable the Venusian surface remains to any visitor.

Studying Venus continues to reshape scientific understanding of how a planet's atmosphere can transform an otherwise Earth-sized world into an inhospitable furnace, offering lessons scientists also apply when examining Earth's own changing climate.

versions.title: Venus: The Hottest Planet in Our Solar System
versions.text:
Venus, recognized as the second planet from the sun and Earth's closest planetary neighbor, frequently appears as the extraordinarily bright point of light visible low in the sky just after sunset or just before sunrise; because its dense clouds reflect such an enormous proportion of sunlight back toward terrestrial observers, Venus ranks as the single brightest planet visible within our entire night sky, outshining every star in its immediate vicinity.

Almost exactly comparable in size to Earth, Venus is occasionally nicknamed Earth's twin by scientists studying planetary formation; yet once researchers began investigating the planet closely using both orbiting and landing spacecraft, they discovered that the two worlds are fundamentally and profoundly nothing alike beneath Venus's swirling, perpetual, unbroken cloud cover.

An extraordinarily thick atmosphere, composed predominantly of carbon dioxide with persistent traces of corrosive sulfuric acid suspended throughout its clouds, envelops the entire planet; this atmosphere presses down upon the surface with roughly ninety times more pressure than Earth's atmosphere exerts at sea level, a magnitude comparable to the crushing pressure experienced nearly a kilometer beneath Earth's oceans. Unlike the gentle water droplets that form clouds on Earth, Venus's clouds consist entirely of this harsh, corrosive acid, capable of damaging numerous materials upon prolonged exposure.

This extraordinarily thick atmosphere traps solar heat near the surface, preventing it from ever effectively radiating back out into the vacuum of space; scientists formally term this phenomenon the greenhouse effect, and on Venus it operates at a truly extreme, runaway level unmatched anywhere else within the solar system. Consequently, Venus has become the solar system's hottest planet by a considerable margin, with surface temperatures exceeding four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, more than sufficient to melt lead; remarkably, Venus remains hotter than Mercury despite the undeniable fact that Mercury orbits considerably closer to the sun and therefore receives substantially more direct solar radiation per unit of surface area.

Venus also rotates in an unusual, backward direction relative to nearly every other planet within the solar system, a phenomenon astronomers formally designate as retrograde rotation; its rotation is also astonishingly slow, since a single Venusian day, representing the duration required for one complete axial spin, actually lasts considerably longer than one entire Venusian year, representing the time required to complete a single orbit around the sun.

Given how extraordinarily harsh surface conditions are, every spacecraft that has successfully landed on Venus has survived only a brief interval, generally under two hours, before extreme heat and crushing atmospheric pressure destroyed its delicate instruments, clear and compelling proof of just how inhospitable the Venusian surface truly remains to any conceivable visitor.

Continued study of Venus has steadily reshaped scientific understanding of how a planet's atmosphere alone can transform an otherwise Earth-sized world into an utterly inhospitable furnace, offering valuable lessons that scientists also apply when modeling Earth's own changing climate and the long-term consequences of greenhouse gases accumulating within an atmosphere.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why a day on Venus is longer than its year?

MID.prompt: Imagine you are a scientist explaining Venus to a younger student. Write a short explanation of three reasons Venus is the hottest planet in our solar system.
checklist: I included three facts from the article about why Venus is so hot.
I explained each fact in my own words.
I organized my explanation with an opening and a closing sentence.
MID.modelAnswer: Venus might look like Earth's twin, but it is actually the hottest planet in our solar system for three main reasons. First, Venus has an extremely thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide, which presses down on the surface with enormous pressure. Second, thick clouds of corrosive acid cover the entire planet and never break apart, unlike the gentle water clouds on Earth. Third, this thick atmosphere traps heat near the surface through the greenhouse effect, so heat cannot escape back into space. Because of these three things working together, Venus stays hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is actually closer to the sun.

HIGH.prompt: Explain, using evidence from the article, why Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the sun. Be sure to describe the role of Venus's atmosphere in your answer.
checklist: I explained at least two specific features of Venus's atmosphere using evidence from the article.
I clearly connected those features to why Venus is hotter than Mercury.
I organized my writing with a clear introduction, body, and conclusion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Although Mercury orbits much closer to the sun, Venus is actually the hottest planet in our solar system because of its extraordinary atmosphere. According to the article, Venus is surrounded by an extremely thick blanket of carbon dioxide gas that presses down on the surface with about ninety times more pressure than Earth's atmosphere. This thick atmosphere, along with its corrosive, acid-filled clouds, traps solar heat near the surface instead of letting it radiate back out into space, a process scientists call the greenhouse effect. Mercury, by contrast, has only a thin, nearly nonexistent atmosphere, so whatever heat it absorbs from the nearby sun quickly escapes back into space. In conclusion, distance from the sun matters less than atmospheric thickness, which is exactly why Venus's runaway greenhouse effect makes it hotter than Mercury despite being farther away.
